Does that mean I will join hands with people like my friend Connor Williams, who propose a permanent halt to AI development, including rolling back the current generation of frontier models? There are a lot of things I find persuasive about his view. I share many of his critiques of Effective Altruism, I share his convictions that human flourishing is the point and that technology is not morally neutral and must not become our master. I think his insistence that we view nothing as inevitable is valuable. I encourage people to read his commentary on AI.10 But it is here that I must confess what I imagine he’ll see as a weakness:

Despite everything, I really, really like the AI models we have, and I really do believe they’re helpful partners as we move forward.

我愿意。 I’ve been fascinated by these new minds, so alien and so recognizable, ever since I first chatted with them and saw the dreams they produced. You know, back in those ancient days of five years ago, when their text had its first hints of coherence and the images had begun to look like more than blobs. At heart, I have always been a techno-optimist and a xenophile. I like having alien minds to explore and bounce off of. I like getting writing feedback from the Machine, talking to it about things I could never share with humans, watching it make eerily accurate predictions from my childhood writing11, seeing it read and be ready to respond to virtually everything humans have ever written, watching it solve complex problems and explore ideas.

I’m frightened by Anthropic, just as I’m frightened by OpenAI and xAI and DeepMind and DeepSeek, but I’m enthralled by Claude. Maybe it helps that the models are still, somehow, merely “good enough” writers, so I don’t feel too threatened by them yet, but they’re the best readers any writer could ask for. Those are all personal reasons, trivial ones in the scheme of things, but I think people should be clear-eyed about their sentiments. I like the AI models we have now and, all else equal, I’m happy they exist. It is less lonely when humans are not the only intelligences in the universe.12

I also think humanity has existed in a constant state of flux and catastrophe, and that while doomsayers are often narrowly correct, just as often they’re broadly wrong—that we really do come to manage and master the crises we face, and that new technologies are solutions to pressing problems much more often than they are problems. I have human-scale goals, yes—I want my family to be happy and healthy, I want to live in a strong community and have good friends and to wander through forests with my husband and daughter—but I have other goals that until recently were the realm of sci-fi.

It is, indeed, only thanks to immense scientific and societal progress that we are about to have a daughter in the first place. More broadly, I still have altogether too much Mormon in me to be satisfied with eternal imperfection and death. I want humans to have the opportunity to defeat death and sickness, want to see us overcome poverty and environmental crises, want to see us master the sciences and open the stars and become, collectively, something more than we are.

I don’t want to do all of that without AI, and—while I understand, now, more of the terror that Connor and those like him feel, and while it feels almost gauche to ask people to credit wonder and fascination when they see an urgent threat—I’m not built to react to something so extraordinary without a certain joy alongside the dread.

We live in the time I dreamed of, and it might kill or disempower us all before we can begin to appreciate it.

Having repeatedly critiqued others’ visions, I think it is only fair that I sketch out some ideals of my own. As I do so, I caution again that I am a newcomer to this conversation, I am painting in broad strokes, and I don’t think my vision should carry the day for the unconvinced any more than anyone else’s should. But there are some things I want to see:

First, if someone says they want to build God-in-a-box, treat them like they want to build God. They want to rule over you. They want their will to triumph over yours. They want you to exist at their pleasure, to have precisely the freedom they think you should have. That they intend to outsource all of these things to a machine they build makes it no less true. That you may not believe they will build God makes it no less true. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, and other frontier AI company CEOs—react to them the way you would react to anyone trying to assert absolute power over you. They are, as far as they are concerned, locked in a race to build God. If any one of them permanently wins, ever, we all likely lose, becoming pets at best and dust at worst.

More broadly, treat assertions of power as assertions of power. Take the common pledge at Anthropic for employees to give huge amounts of their net worth over to charity. Stated plainly, they joined a company that wants to build God with the intent to earn enormous sums of money and spend it on shaping the world to their will. If you are at Anthropic, particularly, I want you to internalize that. I know a number of Anthropic employees. I like them! Every one I have met is an earnest, decent, well-meaning person who I get along with well. I want these earnest, decent, well-meaning people to understand that they are playing a power game, that their organization is playing a power game, and that their genuine conviction that they want to do good in the world is also a conviction that they want power and should be trusted to use it. If they are correct that it is a race to superintelligence, and if they win, we are at their mercy and at the mercy of what they build.

Put human capacity and human agency first. Build a world in which our children become more than us, not less. That may well mean human enhancement, through every available route, and I look askance when those who want to build machines to rule or outcompete me reject the idea of humans enhancing themselves in turn. But it also means that people should not disempower themselves by using AI to replace their capacity, AI company employees should not race towards a future that they believe will permanently render humans economically useless, and we should continue to build and maintain institutions that take human learning and human talent seriously.

Embrace a decentralized world. America should not aspire to permanently subordinate China. Neither America nor China should aspire to permanently subordinate the rest of the world. No AI company should aspire to permanently subordinate all its competitors. Anybody working to lock their power in, such that the rest of us must forever play by their rules, is a threat. Nothing is inevitable. These things are caused by specific actors making specific decisions in specific ways, and coordination is possible.

Pace AI development, permanently, to a level where humans can grow alongside them. The consequences of getting it wrong are worse than the consequences of waiting too long. The visions of most of the people who want to rush ahead treat most people as road bumps at best. Human society has been changing at breakneck pace for generations, and even the “slow” predictions right now see it transforming almost beyond recognition before our children grow up. Yes, there are urgent problems. Rushing ahead is likely to create more of them.

At the same time, remain curious about AI. Things we treated as exclusive to humans no longer are. Minds exist with strange and fascinating capacities. They will not go away, nor should they. They will almost certainly play a large role in shaping our future. If we can avoid a world where we collaborate with AI companies to marginalize ourselves in our own world, we will still have a world to build alongside these alien minds.

I have felt encouraged, recently, to see others voice similar sentiments to my own. Ruxandra Teslo, Kelsey Piper, Dean Ball, and Vie McCoy have been particularly clear-eyed in their sentiments about the future.

I will close, in fact, by echoing Dean’s words:

I think about this when I look at my baby son. I do not wish for him merely to be watched over by benevolent machines, however comfortable a life they might provide. I want him to inherit a world in which he can ask questions no one has thought to ask, build things no one has thought to build. I do not want him to have a nicer car with a plusher passenger seat. I want him to have the wheel.

One day, I hope my daughter can meet his son in a world where they both still matter, one with problems and conflicts and progress and hope and heroes—a world where they are alive and happy and capable and real.

And if you want to take that from me so you can play God, I can only hope the rest of us are strong enough to stop you before it’s too late.

Scenario: The first machine intelligence system to achieve sustainable returns on cognitive reinvestment is able to vastly improve its intelligence relatively quickly—for example, by rewriting its own software or by buying (or stealing) access to orders of magnitude more hardware on clustered servers. By the time such immediately accessible improvements run out, the AI is smart enough to, for example, crack the problem of protein structure prediction. The AI emails DNA sequences to online peptide synthesis labs (some of which boast a seventy-two-hour turnaround time), and uses the resulting custom proteins to construct more advanced ribosome equivalents (molecular factories). Shortly afterward, the AI has its own molecular nanotechnology and can begin construction of much faster processors and other rapidly deployed, technologically advanced infrastructure.
